claims.text: Taking a break from Facebook increases life satisfaction.
Taking a break from Facebook causes emotions to become more positive.
The positive well-being effects of taking a break from Facebook are significantly greater for heavy Facebook users.
The positive well-being effects of taking a break from Facebook are significantly greater for passive Facebook users.
The positive well-being effects of taking a break from Facebook are significantly greater for users who tend to envy others on Facebook.

evidence.description: Demonstrated via a 1-week experiment with 1,095 participants in Denmark comparing a group taking a break from Facebook with a control group continuing use.
Comparison between treatment group (taking a break from Facebook) and control group showed an increase in life satisfaction for the treatment group.
Comparison between treatment group (taking a break from Facebook) and control group showed that participants' emotions became more positive in the treatment group.
Subgroup analysis within the 1-week randomized experiment demonstrated significantly greater well-being increases among heavy Facebook users.
Subgroup analysis within the 1-week randomized experiment demonstrated significantly greater well-being increases among passive Facebook users.
Subgroup analysis within the 1-week randomized experiment demonstrated significantly greater well-being increases among users who tend to envy others on Facebook.

methodologies.name: Randomized controlled experiment
methodologies.description: A 1-week field experiment comparing participants instructed to take a break from Facebook against a control group instructed to continue using Facebook as normal.
conditions: Treatment group: took a 1-week break from Facebook
